planting.note: Pot divisions or nursery starts into a deep container of long-fiber sphagnum moss blended with perlite, pumice, and a little orchid bark, since this sundew sends down an unusually long taproot; keep the mix constantly moist with rain or distilled water and grow in strong light with cool nights.

directions: Restricted in the wild to a single valley in South Africa's Bainskloof mountains, this is by far the largest sundew grown by hobbyists, sending up long, strap-shaped leaves lined with sticky red tentacles capable of trapping moths and other sizable flying insects. Unlike most warm-growing Drosera it responds strongly to shortening days and cooling temperatures by dying back to a tight resting bud, so allow it a cooler, drier rest through winter rather than forcing year-round growth. It tolerates brief heat spikes into the 90s if the root zone stays cool and shaded, but sustained heat without a winter check weakens the plant over time. Established plants benefit from light root-zone fertilization, a rare exception among sundews, which are usually fed no more than the insects they catch themselves.

planting.note: Pot offsets or nursery divisions into a peat-sand or peat-perlite mix kept constantly damp with rain or distilled water; this Cape mountain species prefers cool nights and bright but not scorching light, and sulks in prolonged summer heat above the mid-80s.

directions: First brought into cultivation by British grower Adrian Slack, this Cape Province sundew forms a low rosette of rounded, wedge-shaped leaves that flush deep red and bronze under strong light, edged with glistening sticky tentacles that catch fungus gnats and small flies. As a cool-mountain South African species it has no true winter dormancy but grows best with cooler nighttime temperatures year-round and slows noticeably during the darkest winter months rather than shutting down completely. Keep it frost-free at all times and out of intense midday sun, which can scorch its leaves faster than it colors them. It is a slower grower than the related Cape sundew, so avoid crowding it with more vigorous Drosera in a shared tray.

planting.note: Set divisions or seed-grown plugs into a lean mix of two parts peat to one part each of sand, perlite, and vermiculite, and keep permanently moist with rain or distilled water; like other cold-temperate butterworts it forms a compact winter hibernaculum bud and needs a genuine cold season to thrive long-term.

directions: Native to mountain bogs and wet flushes of the European Alps and Pyrenees, this butterwort produces the largest, showiest flowers of the cold-hardy Pinguicula species — trumpet-shaped, deep violet-blue blooms with a pale throat held well above the sticky, pale-green rosette of leaves each spring. Those leaves lure and slowly digest small flying insects through the same flypaper-like glandular trap used by all butterworts, providing nutrients the poor, mineral-starved bog soil cannot supply. It requires a true freezing winter, dying back to a tight, ice-resistant hibernaculum bud that resumes growth as the ground thaws, so it performs poorly in mild-winter climates without an artificial cold rest. Grow it in a lean, constantly wet peat-based mix in a bog garden, trough, or unheated cold frame, watering only with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water.

common_name: Dixie Lace Pitcher Plant (Red-and-White Laced Sarracenia Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes and set into pure long-fiber sphagnum moss or a 1:1 peat-perlite mix, never fertilized potting soil, and keep the pot standing in a tray of rain or distilled water at all times; this cultivar tolerates a wider swing from wet to briefly drier conditions than most Sarracenia.

directions: Bred at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte from a complex cross of Sarracenia leucophylla, alabamensis, purpurea, and psittacina parentage, Dixie Lace produces sturdy, upright, flat-topped pitchers in white overlaid with a dense red lace-like venation that darkens to maroon as the weather cools in fall. It is a compact, vigorous grower that clumps readily into dense colonies within a few seasons, and as with other pitcher plants it lures insects to the pitcher rim where they slip down the waxy interior walls and are digested to supply nutrients the nutrient-poor bog soil lacks. Established pitchers often persist attractively for two growing seasons rather than dying back after one. Give it full sun for the best color and pitcher production, and allow the plant a natural winter dormancy with reduced water and shorter days, since Sarracenia requires this cold rest to remain vigorous long-term.

common_name: Bug Bat Pitcher Plant (Windowed-Hood Sarracenia Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes and set into pure long-fiber sphagnum moss or a 1:1 peat-perlite mix, never fertilized potting soil, and keep the pot standing in a tray of rain or distilled water at all times.

directions: Selected from a Larry Mellichamp seedling and named for its upright, pointed hoods that shift from cinnamon-red at the top to chartreuse near the base, Bug Bat is dotted along the hood's back with pale translucent windows that glow when backlit by low morning or evening sun. It grows into dense, vigorous colonies within a few seasons and is easier-going than many hybrids, tolerating everything from a saturated bog tray to briefly drier soil between waterings. As with other pitcher plants, insects are drawn to nectar at the rim, slip down the waxy inner walls, and are digested to provide nutrients the poor bog soil cannot. Give it full sun for the strongest coloring and allow a natural winter dormancy with reduced water and shorter days, since Sarracenia requires this cold rest to stay healthy long-term.

planting.note: Divide rhizomes and pot into pure sphagnum moss or a 1:1 peat-perlite mix, keeping the tray sitting in rain or distilled water; give this cultivar extra room compared with standard flytraps since its traps and petioles grow noticeably larger and thicker than the species.

directions: This selection is grown for sheer size, producing some of the largest traps available in cultivation on thick, robust petioles, with color ranging from red to purplish inside the trap under strong light. It is otherwise cared for exactly like any Venus flytrap, potted in pure nutrient-free sphagnum or a peat-perlite blend and kept standing in a tray of rain or distilled water at all times. Provide a cool winter dormancy of several months with reduced light so the rhizome can rest and rebuild the energy needed to produce another season of oversized traps. Divide congested clumps every couple of years both to control crowding and to propagate genetically identical offsets, since the giant trap size is a clonal trait that does not always come true from seed.
